{{smaller block|When abjurations were ''in use'' in this land, the state and law were satisfied if the abjuror came to the sea-side, and waded into the sea when winds and tides resisted.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|use|6674|use}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|If this citizen had not . . . proffered her her diet and lodging under the name of my sister, I could not have told what shift to have made, for the greatest part of my money is revolted; we’ll make more ''use'' of him.
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Constant ''Use'' ev’n Flint and Steel Impairs.</poem>
{{right|''Congreve'', tr. of Ovid’s Art of Love.}}}}
'''2.''' That property of a thing (or character of a person) which renders it suitable for a purpose; adaptability to the attainment of an end; usefulness; availability; utility; serviceableness; service; convenience; help; profit: as, a thing of no ''use''.
{{smaller block|<poem>God made two great lights, great for their ''use''
To man.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vii. 346.}}}}
{{smaller block|We have no doubt that the ancient controversies were of ''use'', in so far as they served to exercise the faculties of the disputants.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Lord Bacon.}}}}
{{smaller block|It [a sitting] might as well last to Sunday morning, as there is no ''use'' in making more than two bites at a cherry.
{{right|''Punch'', No. 2066, p. 64.}}}}
'''3.''' Need for employing; occasion to employ; necessity; exigency; need.
{{smaller block|Be not acknown on ’t [handkerchief]; I have ''use'' for it.
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iii. 3. 319.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Heaven has begun the work,
And blest us all; let our endeavours follow,
To preserve this blessing to our timely ''uses''.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Wife for a Month, v. 1.}}}}
'''4.''' Continued or repeated practice or employment; custom; wont; usage; habit.
{{smaller block|Long ''use'' and experience hath found out many things commodious for man’s life.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), i.}} How ''use'' doth breed a habit in a man!
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., v. 4. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Use'' makes a better soldier than the most urgent considerations of duty—familiarity with danger enabling him to estimate the danger. {{right|''Emerson'', Courage.}}}}

'''5.''' Common occurrence; ordinary experience. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>O Cæsar! these things are beyond all ''use'',
And I do fear them. {{right|''Shak.'', J. C., ii. 2. 25.}}</poem>}}

'''6.''' Interest for money; usury. [Obsolete or archaic.]
{{smaller block|''D. Pedro.'' You have lost the heart of Signior Benedick.
''Beat.'' Indeed, my lord, he lent it me awhile; and I gave him ''use'' for it, a double heart for his single one.
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, ii. 1. 288.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Human life
Is but a loan to be repaid with ''use'',
When He shall call his debtors to account.
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, iii.}}</poem>}}

'''7†.''' That part of a sermon devoted to a practical application of the doctrine expounded.
{{smaller block|<poem>The parson has an edifying stomach, . . .
He hath begun three draughts of sack in doctrines,
And four in ''uses''. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Magnetick Lady, iii. 1.}}</poem>}}

'''8.''' In ''liturgics'', the distinctive ritual and liturgical forms and observances, collectively and singly, of a particular church, diocese, group of dioceses, or community: as, Sarum ''use''; Aberdeen ''use''; Anglican ''use''; Roman ''use''. {{smaller|The term is most frequently applied to the varieties of ritual and liturgical usage in England before the Reformation and to monastic and Roman usage as differing from these, and also to the different local varieties of the ancient Gallican offices. In England the several uses were those of Sarum, York, Hereford, Bangor, Lincoln, etc. These had a common family likeness, and differed considerably from Roman use. The most important of them was Sarum or Salisbury use, which was the form of service compiled about 1085 from various diocesan uses, English and Norman, by St. Osmund, bishop of Salisbury and chancellor of England. The use of Sarum prevailed throughout the greater part of England, and in 1542 it was ordered to be observed throughout the whole province of Canterbury. The Book of Common Prayer, first issued in 1549, and founded mainly on Salisbury use, established a uniform liturgy for the whole Church of England, but, except by implication of certain rubrics, left the exact mode of ritual observance in many respects unprovided for. See ''liturgy'', 3 (4).—'''Sarum use.''' See def. 8.—'''To have no use for.''' (''a'') To have no occasion or need for; be unable to convert to a profitable end; not to want. (''b'') To have no liking for. [U. S.]}}
{{smaller block|“I ''have no use for'' him”—don’t like him.
{{right|''Trans. Amer. Philol. Ass.'', XVII. 46.}}}}

'''To have no use of†.''' {{smaller|Same as ''to have no use for'' (''a'').}}
{{smaller block|Our author calls them “figures to be let,” because the picture ''has no use of'' them.
{{right|''Dryden'', Parallel between Poetry and Painting.}}}}

'''To make use of''', {{smaller|to put in use; employ.}}—'''Use and wont, use and custom,''' {{smaller|the common or customary practice.}}

'''use'''<sup>1</sup> (ūz), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''used'', ppr. ''using''. [< ME. ''usen'', < OF. (and F.) ''user'' = Sp. Pg. ''usar'' = It. ''usare'' = ML. ''usare'', use, employ, practise, etc., freq. of L. ''uti'', pp. ''usus'', use: see ''use''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To employ for the attainment of some purpose or end; avail one’s self of. {{smaller|(''a'') To make use of: as, to ''use'' a plow; to ''use'' a book.}}
{{smaller block|Alwaies in your hands ''vse'' eyther Corall or yellow Amber, or a Chalcedonium, or a sweet Pommander, or some like precious stone, to be worne in a ring vpon the little finger of the left hand.
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 257.}}}}

{{smaller block|Lancelot Gobbo, ''use'' your legs. ''Shak.'', M. of V., ii. 2. 5.}}
{{smaller block|We need not ''use'' long circumstance of words.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Laws of Candy, i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|I am not at my own dispose; I am ''using'' his talents, and all the gain must be his. ''Jer. Taylor'', Holy Living, i. 2.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Since the winds were pleased this waif to blow
Unto my door, a fool I were indeed
If I should fail to ''use'' her for my need.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 266.}}}}

(''b'') To employ; expend; consume: as, to ''use'' flour for food; to ''use'' water for irrigation.
{{smaller block|Instant occasion to ''use'' fifty talents.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., iii. 1. 19.}}}}

(''c'') To practise or employ, in a general way; do, exercise, etc.
{{smaller block|He setteth out the cruelness of the emperor’s soldiers, which they ''used'' at Rome.
{{right|''Tyndale'', Ans. to Sir T. More, etc. (Parker Soc.), p. 188.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>They
Will not, nor cannot, ''use'' such vigilance.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iii. 3. 16.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>We have ''us’d'' all means
To find the cause of her disease, yet cannot.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Custom of the Country, v. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|Deeds and language such as men do ''use''.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man in his Humour, Prol.}}}}
{{smaller block|In prosperity he gratefully admires the bounty of the Almighty giver, and ''useth'', not abuseth plenty.
{{right|''Habington'', Castara, iii.}}}}
{{smaller block|He was questioned about some speeches he had ''used'' in the ship lately, in his return out of England.
{{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, I. 324.}}}}

(''d'') To practise customarily; make a practice of.
{{smaller block|<poem>To dampne a man without answere of word;
And, for a lord, that is ful foul to ''use''.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 402.}}}}
{{smaller block|O what falsehood is ''used'' in England — yea, in the whole world! ''Latimer'', Misc. Selections.}}

{{smaller block|As for Drunkenness, ’tis True, it may be ''us’d'' without Scandal.{{right|''Etherege'', She Would if She Could, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Prodigall in their expence, ''vsing'' dicing, dauncing, dronkennes.{{right|''Lyly'', Euphues, Anat. of Wit, p. 147.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Use'' hospitality one to another.{{right|1 Pet. iv. 9.}}}}
'''2.''' To act or behave toward; treat: as, to ''use'' one well or ill.
{{smaller block|In government it is good to ''use'' men of one rank equally.{{right|''Bacon'', Followers and Friends (ed. 1887).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Oh, brave lady, thou art worthy to have servants,
To be commandress of a family,
Thou knowest how to ''use'' and govern it!</poem>{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Honest Man’s Fortune, iii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>When Pompey liv’d,
He ''us’d'' you nobly; now he is dead, ''use'' him so.</poem>{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', False One, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|’Sdeath! what a brute am I to ''use'' her thus!{{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals, iii. 2.}}}}
'''3.''' To accustom; habituate; render familiar by practice; inure: common in the past participle: as, soldiers ''used'' to hardships.
{{smaller block|About eighteene yeers agone, hauing pupils at Cambridge studious of the Latine tongue, I ''vsed'' them often to write Epistles and Theames together, and dailie to translate some peece of English into Latine.{{right|''Baret'', Alvearie (1580), To the Reader.}}}}
{{smaller block|It will next behoove us to consider the inconvenience we fall into by ''using'' our selves to bee guided by these kind of Testimonies.{{right|''Milton'', Prelatical Episcopacy.}}}}
{{smaller block|If it be one of the baser consolations, it is also one of the most disheartening concomitants of long life, that we get ''used'' to everything.{{right|''Lowell'', Wordsworth.}}}}
'''4.''' To frequent; visit often or habitually.
{{smaller block|And zif the Merchauntes ''useden'' als moche that Contre as thei don Cathay, it wolde ben better than Cathay in a schort while.{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 307.}}}}

{{smaller block|It goes against my conscience to tarry so long in honest company; but my comfort is, I do not ''use'' it.
{{right|''Shirley'', Grateful Servant, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|These many years, even from my youth, have I ''used'' the seas; in which time the Lord God hath delivered me from a multitude of dangers.
{{right|''R. Knox'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 351).}}}}
{{smaller block|“I was better off once, sir,” he did not fail to tell everybody who ''used'' the room. {{right|''Thackeray.''}}}}
'''5†.''' To comport; behave; demean: used reflexively.
{{smaller block|Now will I declare how the citizens ''use'' themselves one to another. {{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia, tr. by Robinson, ii. 5.}}}}
'''6†.''' To have sexual intercourse with. ''Chaucer.'' {{smaller|—'''To use up.''' (''a'') To consume entirely by using; use the whole of.}}
{{smaller block|There is only a certain amount of energy in the present constitution of the sun; and, when that has been ''used up'', the sun cannot go on giving out any more heat.
{{right|''W. K. Clifford'', Lectures, I. 222.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') To exhaust, as one’s means or strength; wear out; leave no force or capacity in: as, the man is completely ''used up''. [Colloq.]}}
{{smaller block|Before we saw the Spanish Main, half were “gastados,” ''used up'', as the Dons say, with the scurvy.
{{right|''Kingsley'', Westward Ho, i.}}
<poem>But what is coffee but a noxious berry,
Born to keep ''used-up'' Londoners awake?</poem>
{{right|''C. S. Calverley'', Beer.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To be accustomed; practise customarily; be in the habit: as, he ''used'' to go there regularly. {{smaller block|Also there, faste by, be .ij. stones; vpon one of them our Sauyoure Criste ''vsed'' to sytte and preche to his disciples.
{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 19.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Sir, if you come to rail, pray quit my house;
I do not ''use'' to have such language given
Within my doors to me.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Coxcomb, iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|As thou ''usest'' to do unto those that love thy name.
{{right|Ps. cxix. 132.}}}}
{{smaller block|So when they came to the door they went in, not knocking; for folks ''use'' not to knock at the door of an inn.
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, ii.}}}}
'''2.''' To be wont; be customary; customarily be, do, or effect something specified.
{{smaller block|<poem>Of Court, it seemes, men Courtesie doe call,
For that it there most ''useth'' to abound.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Madam, your beauty ''uses'' to command,
And not to beg! what is your suit to me?</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>How alter’d is each pleasant nook;—
And ''used'' the dumpy church to look
So dumpy in the spire?</poem>
{{right|''Locker'', Bramble-rise.}}}}
'''3.''' To be accustomed to go; linger or stay habitually; dwell. [Obsolete or provincial.]
{{smaller block|This fellow ''useth'' to the fencing-school, this to the dancing school. {{right|''Dekker'', Gull’s Hornbook, p. 154.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I will give thee for thy food
No fish that ''useth'' in the mud.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Ders er ole gray rat wat ''uses'' ’bout yer, en time atter time he comes out w’en you all done gond ter bed, . . . en me en him talks by de ’our.
{{right|''J. C. Harris'', Uncle Remus, xiv.}}}}
'''4†.''' To communicate; receive the eucharist.

{{smaller block|And the to torches, eueri day in the ȝer, scullen ben light and brennynge at the heye messe at selue auter, from the leuacioun of cristis body sacrid, in til that the priest hāue ''vsud.''
{{right|''English Gilds'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 27.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>When the preste hath don his masse,
''Vsed'', & his hondes wasche,
A-nothur oryson he moste say.</poem>
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 91.}}}}

'''use'''<sup>2</sup> (ūs), ''n.'' [< ME. *''ues'', *''oes'', ''oyss'', < OF. ''ues'', ''oes'', ''uoes'', ''eus'', ''os'', ''oeps'', ''obs'' = Pr. ''obs'' = OSp. ''huevos'' = It. ''uopo'', profit, advantage, use, need, < L. ''opus'', work, labor, need, AL. use, in legal sense: see ''opus''. The word ''use''<sup>2</sup> has been confused with ''use''<sup>1</sup>, with which it is now practically identical.] In ''law'', the benefit or profit (with power to direct disposal) of property—technically of lands and tenements—in the possession of another who simply holds them for the beneficiary; the equitable ownership of lands the legal title to which is in another. {{smaller|He to whose use or benefit the trust is intended enjoys the use of profits, and is called ''cestui que use.'' Since the Statute of Uses, the gift or grant of real property to the use of a person transfers to him directly the legal title; and the term ''trust'' is now commonly used to denote the kind of estate formerly signified by ''use'', so far as the law now permits it to exist. (See ''trust''<sup>1</sup>, 5.) ''Uses'' apply only to lands of inheritance; no use can subsist of leaseholds.}}
{{smaller block|And ''use'' is a trust or confidence reposed in some other.
{{right|''Sir E. Coke'', Com. on Littleton, 272 b.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Use'' seems to be an older word than trust. Its first occurrence in statute law is in 7 Ric. II. c. 12, in the form ''œps.'' In Littleton “confidence” is the word employed. The Statute of Uses seems to regard ''use'', trust, and confidence as synonymous. According to Bacon, it was its permanency that distinguished the ''use'' from the trust.
